---
title: "Stack clocks"
subtitle: "Combine several clocks into one score, and see whether the combination helps"
---

A stack learns weights for several clocks' scores, out of fold, and reports the result next to
the best single clock and the plain mean measured the same way, so the gain (or its absence) is
visible.

## 1. Fit a stack

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Python

```python
res = fa.score(d, clocks="compatible")
st  = fa.stack_clocks(res, target="age",
                      clocks=["horvath2013", "hannum", "dnamphenoage", "zhangen"],
                      method="nnls")

st.weights        # one weight per clock, on standardised scores
st.metrics        # out-of-fold MAE, MedAE, r, slope
st.comparison     # each clock alone, and the plain mean, measured the same way
```

### R

```r
res <- score(d, clocks = "compatible")
st  <- stack_clocks(res, target = "age",
                    clocks = c("horvath2013", "hannum", "dnamphenoage", "zhangen"),
                    method = "nnls")
st$weights
st$comparison
```

:::

## 2. Choose a method

| `method` | What it does | Allowed when |
|---|---|---|
| `"mean"` | The plain average of the scores | Every clock has the same scale type |
| `"nnls"` | Non-negative weights on standardised scores (default) | Always |
| `"ridge"` | Ridge-penalised weights on standardised scores | Always |
| `"cox"` | A Cox model on the scores; `target` is follow-up time and `event_col` the event | You have survival data |

A plain mean of years and a pace has no unit, so it is refused; the learned methods standardise
each clock and take the scale of the target. First-generation clocks are strongly correlated with
each other, which is why the weights come from non-negative least squares or ridge.

## 3. Save it as a clock

```python
st.to_clock("mystack", "my_clocks/")
```

When every clock in the stack is a weighted sum of CpGs followed by constant shifts and
scalings, the stack is itself a weighted sum over all their CpGs. It is written as one
coefficient file that [Add a clock](add.qmd) scores like any other, with coverage checks and a
technical standard error. A stack containing a clock with a nonlinear output (Horvath's
anti-log, a sigmoid) stays in the session: use `st.predict(res)`.

One difference to know: a CpG your data lacks, and that no clock in the stack publishes a
reference value for, is filled with the mean of the present CpGs. For the combined clock that
mean is taken over all of its CpGs rather than each clock's own, so on data missing such CpGs
the collapsed clock and `st.predict(res)` can differ slightly. `warnings.csv` names every such
fill.

## Do not test a group difference on the samples the stack was fitted on

A stack fitted on the same samples you then compare between groups has already seen the answer.
Fit it on one set and test on another. To ask whether a group difference holds across clocks,
use `fa.consensus()` instead ([Age acceleration](../analysis/acceleration.qmd)): it tests rather
than fits.
